property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner getter returns newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment can be invoked successfully but leaves owner unchanged, violating this rule for some fuzzed newOwner values.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address (including the zero address), after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() getter equals newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment leaves owner unchanged and thus violates this property for some fuzzed newOwner inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) sets owner() to newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner() to address(0) for some inputs, violating this property.

For any address that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in owner() equaling the supplied newOwner; the mutant sets owner() to address(0) for some inputs, violating this.

For any non-zero address newOwner and when msg.sender is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) updates owner() to newOwner; the mutant sets owner to address(0) for some newOwner, violating this.

For any call to transferOwnership(newOwner) made by the current owner, the contract's owner() after the call equals the provided newOwner; the mutant instead sometimes sets owner() to address(0), breaking this invariant.

For any caller address X, if X is not the current owner, calling transferOwnership(X) must not change owner (onlyOwner restriction); the mutant removing the require allows non-owners to set owner, breaking this rule.

After any successful call to transferOwnership(newOwner) made by the current owner, the contract's owner must equal the provided newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender, breaking this rule when msg.sender != newOwner.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner (the reference assigns the provided newOwner; the mutant assigns msg.sender so when msg.sender != newOwner the mutant violates this).

For any addresses ownerCaller and newOwner where ownerCaller is the current owner and ownerCaller != newOwner, after ownerCaller calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner must equal newOwner (the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender, breaking the rule when msg.sender != newOwner).

For any addresses currentOwner and newOwner where currentOwner is the contract owner, when currentOwner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner becomes newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender, so when msg.sender != newOwner the mutant violates this rule.
Rule: calling owned() as the current owner must NOT change the owner; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so it mutates owner and breaks this invariant for some owner addresses.

For any caller address that is the contract owner, calling owned() does not change the owner (i.e., owner remains equal to the caller); the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), which changes owner and thus violates this invariant for some owner addresses.

For any address set as owner, calling owned() (a function guarded by onlyOwner) does not change the owner; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), causing owner to change after the call for some owners.

For every initial owner X set via transferOwnership, calling owned() as X preserves the owner (owner remains X); the mutant which assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can change owner during that call and thus can make owner != X after the call.

For any address that is set as owner, calling owned() while pranked as that same owner preserves the owner (owner remains equal to that address); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can change owner and thus violates this invariant for some fuzzed owner addresses.

For every caller address, calling owned() on the correct contract succeeds (does not revert) iff msg.sender == owner; the mutant inverts the check so owned() instead succeeds for non-owners and reverts for the owner, breaking that rule for many caller addresses.

For any caller that is the current owner and any candidate newOwner address, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's public owner must equal newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment breaks this by leaving owner unchanged for some inputs.

For any caller that is the current owner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner getter equals the supplied newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to address(0) for some inputs (when caller is owner), violating this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() equaling the provided newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to address(0) for some newOwner values, breaking this rule.

For all callers, only the current owner can successfully change C.owner via transferOwnership; the mutant removes the onlyOwner check allowing some non-owner callers to change owner, violating this invariant.

For every caller and target newOwner, only the current owner can change C.owner via transferOwnership (calls by non-owners do not change owner); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so some non-owner call can change owner.

For all callers addr and newOwner addresses, if the caller is not the current owner then calling transferOwnership(addr, newOwner) must not change the owner (only the owner can transfer ownership); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so some non-owner caller can change owner.

For every caller and proposed newOwner, if the caller is not the current owner then after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner remains unchanged; the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so some non-owner caller can change owner.

For every caller and proposed newOwner, if the caller is not the current owner then calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must revert (only owner can call); the mutant removes the require check causing some non-owner calls to succeed and change owner.

For any caller address A, if A is the current owner then calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds and updates owner to newOwner; the mutant requiring msg.sender==address(0) prevents legitimate owners (non-zero EOAs) from passing the guard and thus breaks this rule for some inputs.
